sentences.text: The place I’m visiting this time needs no introduction...
and that’s actually part of the problem.
Hello Stonehenge!
I’ve wanted to film this video for years.

Finding the time, the day, the weather, the person to guide me, getting clearance from English Heritage, who manage Stonehenge, there were only a few possible days on the road trip when I was near Wiltshire, in the south-west of England, and this time, it all happened to line up.
So, at sunrise, one day after the equinox, before any of the crowds arrived, I found myself with Win, Curator of Stonehenge.
Just me and one single camera, so, this may be a little jumpy at times.
We’re going to step inside the stone circle, we’re going to learn a number of things that surprised me about the history, and we’re going to answer the question: why can’t you touch it anymore?
Actually, why can’t most people even get near it?
And I was gonna say that being here so early in the morning is a special privilege.
And it sort of is, but this is a thing that folks can sign up for and do.
Yes, yes, you can book special stone circle access visits.
They’re a bit more expensive, but well worth it, ’cos you actually get to go inside the stones.
I’ve never been this close to Stonehenge. I’ve not been off the road before.
Let me show the audience what I can see here.
So, just off in the distance, it’s gonna be just a few pixels on here, but you can see the headlights of the cars over there.
-Yeah. -And there...
is Stonehenge, plus a photographer.

The first time you take the A303 road that’s one of the main routes from London down to the south-west of England, you may well be very happy that there’s a traffic jam in that area, ’cos from your car window, you’ll get a good, long, slow look at Stonehenge!
And then every other time you take that road, you’ll be really annoyed by the traffic jam caused by all the damn tourists gawping at Stonehenge.
Should a major road have been built through an archaeological site?
No, not by modern standards.
But you can see in this aerial photo from 1928, not only did there used to be two roads next to it, but the Army built an airfield there!
You could just park up by the side of the road, stretch your legs, go see Stonehenge, maybe a plane would take off.
Things have changed a lot, but...
not that much, ’cos you can still see the vehicles speeding by.
There are lots of things from history that are only famous now because they got discovered in the 20th or even the 21st century.
This has been famous for a long time.
It’s not like the Mona Lisa, where at some point it’s like, “Oh, it’s a painting, it’s a painting. Oh, it’s the painting.”
-Yeah. -This has always been famous.
It has, and the Romans visited it.
And it occurs in medieval documents.
Even Geoffrey of Monmouth is referring to it.
You know, Merlin and all the rest of it. How he brought the stones here.
So, it is one of the wonders of Britain and was described as such during the medieval period.
So, yes, it’s always been here, always been famous.
I mean, nowadays it’s become very much a tick box as far as tourists are concerned. -Right. Yes.
You know, so now we get about 1.3 million visitors here.
But when I was a kid, and lots of people share this story, they used to be able to walk inside the stones.
There’s footage of a druid ceremony from 1963: not only are the spectators walking in and around and touching the stones, people are climbing up on top of them to watch!
Turns out, that does a lot of damage.
When you look at the stones here, do you see the tide mark?
-The tide mark? Oh! -There’s like a tide mark.
So, at about the level where an adult could reach?
-Yes. -There’s no moss, there’s no lichen on it.
There’s no lichen on it. Well, there’s some.
We headed over the rope and into the stone circle.

And despite all the photos and videos I’ve seen of Stonehenge in my lifetime, Win had pointed out something obvious that I’d never noticed before: there’s a line about two or three metres up, where the colour changes.
That’s not natural.
That’s because humans have rubbed away the moss and lichen that’s growing on the stones.
So, this belongs to the middle of the 26th century BC.
- -I know it sounds really freaky, but it’s modern!
26th century BC.
26th century BC. Well, let me put that in context.
Farming starts around 4000 BC in this country.
And the earliest humans we got, any idea, in Britain?
-Okay. -Okay.
-So, when you say relatively modern? -It’s modern!
I mean, as an archaeologist... - ...the farming period, when farming comes in at 4000 BC is just really quite recent.
Compared with the very long hunter-gatherer phase of people in Britain.
It wasn’t continuous, but from 900,000-ish, we’ve got evidence of stone tool making and that kind of thing.
So, 4000 BC is when farming starts.
So, the first phase of Stonehenge is a thousand years after that.
That’s the first phase?
So, the first phase is 3000 BC, with the bank and ditch and a circle.
But 400 years later or so, they are building these big sarsen stones.
And these come from about 20, 30 miles away.
West Woods on the Marlborough Downs.
How do they know how old it is?
You can’t carbon-date rock.
But you can carbon-date the remains, wood, charcoal, bones found in archaeological digs there, you can look at the layers of soil deposits over the millennia, and work out the story from that.
So, how deep do they go?
I know, obviously, cannot touch the stones, cannot get too close to the stones, but how deep do they go down?
They go considerably deep.
In some cases, they become very unstable ’cos they weren’t deep enough.
They vary.
And interestingly, studies that were done back in 2012 show that there are smaller stones slightly on this side, they’re slightly shorter because the land is higher here than it is over there.
So, they squared it at the top?
-So, the top is level. -Right.
So, they’ve got bigger stones on the, you know, taller stones on the other side.
I see what you mean about the tide mark on this!
-Oh, yeah. -That’s such a good example.
So, at about the point where, again, do not touch the stone...
...at about the point where an average adult can reach with your hand, all the lichen just stops. Yes.
And that is, lichens take, in some cases, you know, hundreds of years to develop.
-Yeah. -So, you know, this...
The stone circle was closed off to the general public back in 1977.
So, there’s been some time for this to recover.
But, as you can see, it hasn’t recovered as much as the rest.
You can see how the stones are shaped, if you know what to look for: Win pointed out the long grooves along one of the fallen stones: that’s Neolithic stone shaping there.
But that’s not the only carving that’s happened.
The survey that was done in 2012 also showed that there was a lot of damage to the stones.
People coming in and chipping stones off.
We can see that.
I think this one here shows some damage on the corner here.
This is where they chip pieces off.
I think it’s these bits here.
You see, the easiest place is to knock ’em off the corners.
-Yeah. -And I think that’s...
That’s at about the height that...
Yeah, exactly. I think that’s damage.
Someone’s...
I read somewhere that sometimes they even...
you could even borrow a hammer or rent a hammer to do it, you know.
Come and help yourself.
People used to just wander in for centuries.
And it was just seen as a curiosity.
And there wouldn’t be much traffic across, you know, across Salisbury Plain, you know, back in the 17th century.
It would be a fairly isolated place.
So, yeah, you might just pop across the stones and grab yourself a souvenir.
More than that, I can see graffiti very clearly.
Absolutely.
Even Sir Christopher Wren put his name over there.
-No! -He did, I’ll show you.
Sir Christopher Wren, born 1632 in Wiltshire, near Stonehenge, perhaps the greatest architect in English history, designed St Paul’s Cathedral.

And to be fair to him, perhaps it was someone else who carved a cross, the traditional abbreviation for Christopher, and the word “Wren” into Stonehenge, using incredibly precise serifed text. Who knows!
Here we are.
Yes, I can see that!
“Wren”.
Sir Christopher Wren, builder of the great St Paul’s Cathedral, thinks, “Well, I shall put my name on Stonehenge.”
My first thought was: the ego required to do that!
A permanent mark left on history, a lasting impression.

Speaking of things that leave a lasting impression: When you travel abroad, there’s a fair chance that a minute or so after you get to a new country, by road or train or plane, you’ll get a friendly, but also slightly threatening, text from your mobile provider
telling you what extortionate sum they’re going to charge you for using the internet on your phone.
Which is why I have an account with Saily.
They’ll give you an eSIM, another data connection on your phone.

And you don’t need a new one per country: you install a single eSIM on your phone once, pick a data plan for whichever country or region you're going to before you set off, and the moment your plane lands, in Canada, or more than a hundred other countries,
your data connects automatically And on almost every modern phone, your regular home SIM card stays active at the same time, so you don’t miss incoming calls or texts from home.

Saily now has Shared Plans, too, so if you’re travelling with family or friends one person can buy a data plan and share that allowance with up to four other people, so they don’t have to drain their battery being the portable wi-fi hotspot all day.

And you can also get a US phone number, in case you're travelling around North America and need a local number to book a table, or get an SMS code for somewhere that doesn’t understand that some people’s phone numbers don’t start with +1.
Which has happened to me!
I couldn’t book a ticket for something a couple of months ago because I didn’t have a North American number!
Set it up before your next flight: download the Saily app by scanning the QR code or clicking the link below, and remember to use the code TOMSCOTT at checkout for a discount on your first plan.
Was that ad part of this video’s history, or just graffiti, daubed on?
I’ll leave that to the future.
Because for Christopher Wren’s graffiti I had to check: was it ego?
Or is that just how it feels from a 21st-century perspective?
Is it arrogance?
Or they were just in a pile of stones?
You know, people didn’t quite respect them.
I think it’s partly because they thought at that time, they were Roman.
Yeah? So...
And there’s even something that dates to 3,600 BC over there, they thought was a Roman racecourse, so they called it a “cursus”.
And they didn’t understand prehistory.
It’s not really until the 1850s that people start to understand prehistory at all.
It was all compressed into a couple of hundred years before the Romans, with some druids thrown in and all the rest of it, you know.
And now we understand this incredible prehistory of humans.
So, we don’t know who...
I-E-W?
I-F-W?
Yeah, no idea.
But at some point, someone has carved their initials.
To be fair, carved them very well into that.
Yes, they’ve done that kind of professionally, yes.
And again, with the serifs on the tops of the letters, you can suggest that it’s probably 18th century, maybe 17th, something like that.
What’s the mark just here?
Well, this is, I’ve forgotten the name, John somebody, do you see I-O-H?
-Yes. -L-Y-D, etc.
I forgot who it actually was, but that’s a really early one.
But here, do you see that shape there?
Is that a cross?
-It’s a dagger, actually. -A dagger!
It’s a dagger.
This is an early Bronze Age dagger, somewhere between about 1750 and 1500 BC.
And these stones, there’s four stones that are covered with lots of these axes.
Four of the stones have carvings that are so faint now they can only be seen with modern laser scans, fractions of a millimetre deep, on the verge of being eroded into random noise.
There’s something about the scale of... oh, don’t touch the stones...
Being dwarfed by this.
There is something about being just shadowed by something this big and this heavy that has stood here for this long.
-Yeah. -I can see...
why this became a thing because people could come in here.
The frustrating thing is, I wasn’t really impressed by Stonehenge before I got inside.
It’s famous, sure, but it’s just a stone circle, Britain’s got loads of them, and you can generally just walk up to them.
In Avebury, a little way away, they’ve got a huge stone circle with a village and a pub in the middle of it.
They’re not nearly as careful with their stones, admittedly, because they don’t have to be.
To me, Stonehenge was just something that caused an annoying traffic jam when I’m driving on the A303.
And then I stood inside, with millennia-old stones towering over me and...
I got it.
And remember, Stonehenge now is a fraction of what it once was.
So, that heel stone is crucial.
And it may actually have been here first, of all the stones.
Because there are random sarsen stones littering Salisbury Plain.
And they may have put that one up and seen some kind of solar alignment at the time.
So, it could be even earlier. We don’t know.
So, these are the trilithons, these really tall ones.
Okay, so we have the outer stone circle, well, outer-ish.
-Indeed. -And then we have tall one here.
Yeah, and tall one there. So...
Tall one there.
So, let’s move round from the left-hand side, round there, and then there was a massive one in the middle.
The Great Trilithon.
And you can see one of them still standing, the other one has fallen.
Trilithon is the name for...?
Three stones.
-Two up, one across. -Yeah, tri, three, lithon, stones.
Took me a second.
Oh, yeah, “lith”. Right. -Lith. Yeah.
“Lithos” is the Greek word for stone: hence “monolith”, one big stone, and “trilithon”, three big stones.
Also, the many, many medical words ending in “-lith” for when your body makes a stone where a stone shouldn’t be.
The next thing Win said...
I’m not going to say it was startling, it’s obvious in hindsight, but again, I had never thought about how Stonehenge was put together.
The biggest trilithon was in the middle.
One of those still standing, and you can see the mortice joint on the top?
-Oh! -So, they sat inside the hole down here.
And the hole over there.
Do you see how they are jointed?
Yes! I feel like I should have known that Stonehenge was not simply rocks piled on top of rocks.
I feel like, in my research, at some point I should have figured that out.
-Yeah. -But that’s a joint.
That is a joint, a mortise and tenon joint.
In some cases, you get elongated grooves.
So, the normal thing is to have a mortise and tenon like that, and then a groove at the other end.
I guess so you could slide them around. There was a bit of give in it.
So, yes, so that’s the great trilithon up there.
And interestingly, they made a mistake. They started to put one on the other side.
So, they did!
By mistake.
You can imagine the annoyance.
“Lads, lads, we’ve...”
“We’ve put it in the wrong place!”
“I’ve spent two days carving this!”
Quite.
Whoever you are watching this, I hope that any mistakes you make in life aren’t still being used as a punchline thousands of years later.
They used joints, a raised part in one stone, a matching hole in another.
So, there are mortise and tenon joints, presumably, under there.
-You can see one on the top there. -Oh, you can!
There’s a little bump on that left-hand stone.
Indeed.
Which would have connected to the next one.
-Yeah. -It seems so obvious, once you point it out, that, of course, all this was connected.
Of course, this was going to be one big...
we don’t know how far it went.
It might have been a full circle?
Well, we think it probably was.
There’s been some debate as to whether it was ever finished.
But we think it probably was because we can see recently, I can’t show you now because the rain has come back, but in the dry summer we’ve had, you could see the parch marks of the holes.
So, where there are stones missing, you can actually see where they used to be because of sort of yellow patches in the grass.
So, it would probably have been a full circle with mortise and tenon joints.
-Yeah. -And every single one of those stones would have had a...
cap? I don’t know what to call it. -All jointed. Lintel.
-Lintel. -Those have all got lintels, yes.
-So, that would have just continued... -So, that’s a full circle.
Yeah. -...onwards?
And then on the inside...
inside you’ve got the great, there are five trilithons.
So, we’re looking at one, two.
There’s the missing one.
-Which was the tallest, as you can see. -Yeah.
-The really big humdinger in the middle. -Well, it’s not missing, it’s just, it’s there. -Yeah, yeah, quite.
And then there were two more over here.
So, this horseshoe of, you know, two pairs on that side, two pairs on this side, and a big one in the middle.
There are even suggestions of different arrangements over the years: there are parch marks, disturbances in the ground where the grass doesn’t grow as well, that means stones might have been moved.
Which actually raises a big question: how did prehistoric people, thousands of people, with no writing and no telecommunication, do something like this?
Oh, that sunrise!
Oh, it’s fantastic, isn’t it?
You can’t cram thousands of people in here.
Yet thousands of people built it.
Huh.
So, that doesn’t necessarily mean we have a hierarchical society.
We don’t think we do at that stage.
We don’t see any other evidence of a highly stratified society.
You know, lots of posh people and poor people and everybody in between.
It seems to be a kind of egalitarian society.
But we don’t have any sign of settlement around here.
They’re not living locally.
They’re probably coming from long distances.
And the analysis of the teeth in the cattle, particularly, but also the pigs, is showing that some of them, or many of them, are coming from areas of granite.
They’re coming from Wales or Dartmoor.
So, they are travelling... -Analysis of the teeth in the cattle?
So, the isotopes, it’s the balance of oxygen, strontium, and nitrogen isotopes that allow you to triangulate where people have grown up.
So, when your teeth are forming as a child, you’re drinking the local water.
And in that water is a signature of the geology, the local geology.
Wow!
So, we can now see where these people are coming from to come to Stonehenge.
We know they’re coming for midwinter solstice.
How do they navigate?
You know, if you live in the back of beyond, say in Devon or Wales, how would you find your way to Stonehenge for the big midwinter celebration?
How would you know about Stonehenge?
-Exactly. - There’s terrific communication going on.
What everything tells me, you know, people always ask about, “Gosh, how do they put these stones up?” You know, and...
That feels like a relatively easy job compared to finding...
Yeah.
Through a network of unsigned paths that on local knowledge...
Yes.
...via landmarks and routes passed down person to person...
this is before writing or at least, no writing survived.
No writing at all, no, no.
Do we know that writing hadn’t been invented, or could it have been that none has survived?
We’re pretty sure it hasn’t been invented at this stage, yeah, yeah.
For me, the elephant in the room about Stonehenge is the social networks.
It’s the fact that they could mobilise very large numbers of people, and they could organise them.
So, we’re seeing incredible social complexity.
You know, anybody can work out how you put some stones up, you know.
One person can do that, with a... give them a lever big enough!
Well, levers and ramps, and we can see from the holes in the ground where we’ve excavated, you know, how they were creating ramps to put the stones on the tops.
We can do a lot of that.
I mean, that isn’t so important to me.
What’s important to me is what it tells you about Stone Age Society.
You know that they can organise vast numbers of people.
You know, the logistics in these operations were absolutely massive.

Imagine that you and your friends, scattered around the country, have no way to communicate other than person to person, and there’s not a single signpost or atlas in existence because writing has not yet been invented.
How would you even start to meet up?
I don’t know.
I don’t think most people today would know.
Obviously, as the days get shorter, they’ll start to realise that they need to be at Stonehenge for the midwinter celebrations.
But when is that? When exactly is it?
When exactly is it?
And how do you time that journey?
Exactly. Yes.

And they’re going to start, if they’re walking from Wales or Devon or anywhere, maybe from hundreds of miles beyond, because this seems to have been a major site for Britain, you’re gonna have to time your journey for a long time before.
And where are you going to stay in midwinter?
There was no physical infrastructure for travel.
There was no physical infrastructure for anything.
There was just...
trust.
They are very closely connected, and they’ve got incredible communication structures to be able to time their efforts and to time their celebrations in the time of the year.
That’s the big question of Stonehenge.
Not how it was built.
But for millennia, people have come here, sometimes leaving marks behind, sometimes burying their dead, sometimes...
well, we don’t know.
No records have survived because there were no records, and there was no writing.
And when Stonehenge fell out of use, and became a curiosity, something that most people might have heard of, but would never see in their lifetimes...
that was fine.
But what happens when there are telecommunications, and there is a bucket list for tourists coming to Britain, and what happens when 1.3 million people a year visit Stonehenge?
A lot of the inside of the stone circle has been excavated, but we really don’t want to touch any more of it because it’s so precious.
That’s where all the information is.
If we let 1.3 million visitors hammer that every year, the compression in the ground is going to be very, very destructive of all the scientific knowledge we can still get out of it.
But if we let everybody go in, it would pummel the archaeology.
They’re still coming up with new scientific techniques.
They’re still trying to save the lichens that protect the rocks, which have scientific and ecological value themselves.
Every touch, every single visitor, damages the site just a little.
A few thousand people a year?
Not a problem, compared to time and weather and wildlife.
More than a million?
It just doesn’t scale.
Conservation is the most important aspect of our work.
And that’s what English Heritage does.
We have 400 monuments across England, and the most important thing is to preserve them, but also to bring public access as much as we can.
And it’s always a balance between access and conservation.
The whole site was paved with gravel for a while, but those tiny stones would get kicked up and cause damage to the big ones.
People are allowed in, on the solstice, some of them do touch the stones despite being asked not to.
And all those crowds...
that would be Stonehenge at peak times, every bright summer day, every tourist coming by.
It can’t survive that.
It wasn’t surviving that.
And then I had a question that is currently just theoretical: what happens if a stone becomes unstable?
Would they let it fall? Or would they shore it up?
Because that’s been done before.
In 1958, there were cranes on site at Stonehenge, lifting up rocks and moving them and stabilising them.
And one of the rocks is now held up with concrete!
That’s not subtle!
Here’s the real stone.
That’s...
There’s the concrete.
That’s just a...
that’s a solid lump of...
I mean, we’re talking modern in relative parlance here.
-Yeah. -That’s just a solid lump of modern concrete that someone’s chucked...
-Yeah, just to make it safe. -Just to make it safe.
I’m being a bit harsh to the previous restoration work there, that stone would have fallen over and probably done more damage if it hadn’t been carefully fixed up with concrete.
It’s just a handful that have been re-erected or stabilised like this.
Yeah, we don’t do this sort of thing lightly.
On this one here...
Well, I’m guessing English Heritage these days doesn’t do that sort of thing at all.
I think we’d do it. Well, it would be an interesting question.
I mean, that’s sort of my job as curator that I’d have to advise, you know, because if you suddenly found out one of these big ones was about to fall, what would you do?
- -It’s an important debate to have. But...
There is no good answer there, is there?
No, I think you might well go down the concrete road for that.
Yeah, so some of the stones have been put back and things.
And at least that concrete restoration is real.
They’ve not faked it up, they’ve not shaped the concrete to look like it’s old.
It’s honest, for now and for other archaeologists in the future, who in thousands of years may say, well, we know they still revered Stonehenge in the early Anthropocene, it was known and visited...
because we can tell that in the 20th, 21st century, they repaired it.
Next time, or right now on Nebula: I step inside a mysterious giant that was born in a barn.

vi: Địa điểm tôi ghé thăm lần này không cần giới thiệu...
và đó thực ra là một phần của vấn đề.
Xin chào Stonehenge!
Tôi đã muốn quay video này suốt nhiều năm.

Tìm được thời gian, ngày, thời tiết, người hướng dẫn, xin phép từ English Heritage, tổ chức quản lý Stonehenge, trong chuyến đi đường dài chỉ có vài ngày khả dĩ khi tôi ở gần Wiltshire, ở tây nam nước Anh, và lần này, mọi thứ tình cờ khớp nhau.
Vậy nên, lúc bình minh, một ngày sau ngày xuân phân/thu phân, trước khi đám đông đến, tôi ở cùng Win, người phụ trách Stonehenge.
Chỉ có tôi và một chiếc máy quay duy nhất, nên đôi lúc hình có thể hơi rung.
Chúng ta sẽ bước vào bên trong vòng tròn đá, sẽ biết một số điều khiến tôi ngạc nhiên về lịch sử, và sẽ trả lời câu hỏi: vì sao bạn không còn được chạm vào nó nữa?
Thực ra, vì sao hầu hết mọi người thậm chí không thể lại gần?
Và tôi định nói rằng ở đây vào sáng sớm thế này là một đặc quyền.
Và đúng là vậy phần nào, nhưng đây là việc mọi người có thể đăng ký và làm.
Vâng, vâng, bạn có thể đặt các chuyến tham quan tiếp cận đặc biệt vòng tròn đá.
Chúng đắt hơn một chút, nhưng rất đáng, vì bạn thực sự được vào bên trong các tảng đá.
Tôi chưa bao giờ ở gần Stonehenge thế này. Trước giờ tôi chưa từng rời khỏi con đường.
Để tôi cho khán giả xem tôi thấy gì ở đây.
Vậy, ở ngay phía xa kia, trên này sẽ chỉ là vài điểm ảnh, nhưng bạn có thể thấy đèn pha ô tô ở đằng kia.
-Vâng. -Và đó...
là Stonehenge, cùng một nhiếp ảnh gia.
